using the equivalence principle to define the actual injected currents.\n219\t\n220\t     Notes\n221\t     -----\n222\t\n223\t        For the injection to work as expected (i.e. to reproduce the required ``E`` and ``H`` fields),\n224\t        the field data must decay by the edges of the source plane, or the source plane must span the entire\n225\t        simulation domain and the fields must match the simulation boundary conditions.\n226\t\n227\t        The equivalent source currents are fully defined by the field components tangential to the\n228\t        source plane. For e.g. source normal along ``z``, the normal components (``Ez`` and ``Hz``)\n229\t        can be provided but will have no effect on the results, and at least one of the tangential\n230\t        components has to be in the dataset, i.e. at least one of ``Ex``, ``Ey``, ``Hx``, and ``Hy``.\n231\t\n232\t        .. TODO add image here\n233\t\n234\t        ..\n235\t            TODO is this generic? Only the field components tangential to the custom source plane are needed and used\n236\t            in the simulation. Due to the equivalence principle, these fully define the currents that need to be\n237\t            injected. This is not to say that the normal components of the data (:math:`E_x`, :math:`H_x` in our example)\n238\t            is lost or not injected. It is merely not needed as it can be uniquely obtained using the tangential components.\n239\t\n240\t        ..\n241\t            TODO add example for this standalone\n242\t            Source data can be imported from file just as shown here, after the data is imported as a numpy array using\n243\t            standard numpy functions like loadtxt.\n244\t\n245\t        If the data is not coming from a ``tidy3d`` simulation, the normalization is likely going to be arbitrary and\n246\t        the directionality of the source will likely not be perfect, even if both the ``E`` and ``H`` fields are\n247\t        provided. An empty normalizing run may be needed to accurately normalize results.\n248\t\n249\t        To create this empty simulation it is recommended that users create a simulation with no structures but just a flux\n250\t        monitor (``tidy3D.FluxMonitor``) next to the custom source, ensuring that the flux monitor is at least one grid cell\n251\t        away from the source. Moreover, for accurate normalization, users must ensure that the same grid is used to run\n252\t        the original simulation as well as the empty simulation. The total flux calculated at the flux monitor of the empty\n253\t        simulation can then be used for proper normalization of results after ``tidy3d`` simulation.\n254\t\n255\t        The coordinates of all provided fields are assumed to be relative to the source center.\n256\t        In other words, the dataset is interpreted in a local coordinate frame centered at\n257\t        :attr:`center`; when injecting/interpolating, the simulation-space coordinates are\n258\t        ``dataset_coords + center``. This means the same dataset can be translated in space by\n259\t        changing :attr:`center` without modifying dataset coordinates.\n260\t        If only the ``E`` or only the ``H`` fields are provided, the source will not be directional,\n261\t        but will inject equal power in both directions instead.\n262\t\n263\t    Example\n264\t    -------\n265\t    >>> from tidy3d import ScalarFieldDataArray, GaussianPulse\n266\t    >>> import tidy3d as td\n267\t    >>> pulse = GaussianPulse(freq0=200e12, fwidth=20e12)\n268\t    >>> x = np.linspace(-1, 1, 101)\n269\t    >>> y = np.linspace(-1, 1, 101)\n270\t    >>> z = np.array([0])\n271\t    >>> f = [2e14]\n272\t    >>> coords = dict(x=x, y=y, z=z, f=f)\n273\t    >>> scalar_field = ScalarFieldDataArray(np.ones((101, 101, 1, 1)), coords=coords)\n274\t    >>> dataset = FieldDataset(Ex=scalar_field)\n275\t    >>> custom_source = CustomFieldSource(\n276\t    ...     center=(1, 1, 1),\n277\t    ...     size=(2, 2, 0),\n278\t    ...     source_time=pulse,\n279\t    ...     field_dataset=dataset)\n280\t\n281\t    Creating an empty simulation with no structures with ``FluxMonitor`` for normalization but with the same grid as the\n282\t    original simulation.\n283\t\n284\t    Example\n285\t    -------\n286\t    >>> Flux_monitor = td.FluxMonitor(\n287\t    ...     center=(0, 0, 0),\n288\t    ...     size=(3, 3, 3),\n289\t    ...     freqs=f,\n290\t    ...     name=\"Flux\",\n291\t    ...     )\n292\t    >>> sim = td.Simulation(\n293\t    ...       center=[0,0,0],\n294\t    ...       size=(4, 4, 4),\n295\t    ...       structures=[],\n296\t    ...       sources=[custom_source],\n297\t    ...       monitors=[],\n298\t    ...       run_time = 1e-6,\n299\t    ...       shutoff=1e-6,\n300\t    ...    )\n301\t    >>> sim_empty = sim.updated_copy(monitors = [Flux_monitor],  # This can be\n642\t        computed in our eigenmode solver :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver` and implement the mode simulation in\n643\t        FDTD.\n644\t\n645\t        Mode sources are normalized to inject exactly 1W of power at the central frequency.\n646\t\n647\t        The modal source allows you to do directional excitation. Illustrated\n648\t        by the image below, the field is perfectly launched to the right of the source and there's zero field to the\n649\t        left of the source. Now you can contrast the behavior of the modal source with that of a dipole source. If\n650\t        you just put a dipole into the waveguide, well, you see quite a bit different in the field distribution.\n651\t        First of all, the dipole source is not directional launching. It launches waves in both directions. The\n652\t        second is that the polarization of the dipole is set to selectively excite a TE mode. But it takes some\n653\t        propagation distance before the mode settles into a perfect TE mode profile. During this process,\n654\t        there is radiation into the substrate.\n655\t\n656\t        .. image:: /_static/img/mode_vs_dipole_source.png\n657\t\n658\t        **Practical Advice**\n659\t\n660\t        Place mode sources in waveguide sections with a uniform cross-section. The mode profile is\n661\t        computed assuming translational invariance (or constant bend radius) along the injection axis.\n662\t        For bent waveguides, set ``bend_radius`` and ``bend_axis`` accordingly. Avoid placing mode\n663\t        sources at tapers, junctions, or other locations where the cross-section is changing.\n664\t\n665\t        .. gradients.\"\"\"\n    field_type, component_axis = parse_source_field_component(field_name, source_name=source_name)\n    if component_axis == injection_axis:\n        raise ValueError(\n For 'chebyshev', a Chebyshev interpolation is used with 'num_freqs' terms \"\n        \"(max 20). For 'pole_residue', the mode solver samples at 'num_freqs' uniform \"\n        \"frequencies and fits ceil((num_freqs - 1) / 3) poles; higher values provide denser \"\n        \"sampling and more poles for the fit (max 50).\",\n        ge=1,\n        le=50,\n    )\n\n    broadband_method: Literal[\"chebyshev\", \"pole_residue\"] = Field(\n        \"chebyshev\",\n        title=\"Broadband Method\",\n        description=\"Method for representing the frequency dependence of the injected field. \"\n        \"'chebyshev' uses Chebyshev polynomial interpolation (default). \"\n        \"'pole_residue' uses a pole-residue (vector fitting) decomposition with \"\n        \"auxiliary differential equation (ADE) time stepping. The pole-residue method \"\n        \"can be more accurate for highly dispersive modes and uses fewer broadband terms \"\n        \"than frequency samples.\",\n    )\n\n    @model_validator(mode=\"after\")\n    def _validate_num_freqs_limit(self) -> Self:\n        \"\"\"Enforce method-specific bounds on num_freqs.\"\"\"\n        if self.broadband_method == \"chebyshev\" and self.num_freqs > 20:\n            raise SetupError(\n                f\"For broadband_method='chebyshev', 'num_freqs' must be <= 20, got {self.num_freqs}.\"\n            )\n        if self.broadband_method == \"pole_residue\" and self.num_freqs < 3:\n            raise SetupError(\n                f\"For broadband_method='pole_residue', 'num_freqs' must be >= 3, got {self.num_freqs}. \"\n                \"The vector fitting algorithm requires more frequency samples than fit coefficients.\"\n            )\n        return self\n\n    @cached_property\n    def frequency_grid(self) -> NDArray:\n        \"\"\"Frequency grid used to approximate frequency dependence.\n\n        For Chebyshev: returns ``num_freqs`` Chebyshev-spaced points.\n        For pole_residue: returns ``num_freqs`` uniformly spaced points.\n        \"\"\"\n        if self.num_freqs == 1:\n            return np.array([self.source_time._freq0])\n        freq_min, freq_max = self.source_time.frequency_range_sigma(sigma=CHEB_GRID_WIDTH)\n        if self.broadband_method == \"pole_residue\":\n            return np.linspace(freq_min, freq_max, self.num_freqs)\n        return self._chebyshev_freq_grid(freq_min, freq_max)\n\n    def _chebyshev_freq_grid(self, freq_min: float, freq_max: float) -> NDArray:\n        \"\"\"A Chebyshev grid based on a minimum and maximum frequency.\"\"\"\n        freq_avg = 0.5 * (freq_min + freq_max)\n        freq_diff = 0.5 * (freq_max - freq_min)\n        uni_points = (2 * np.arange(self.num_freqs) + 1) / (2 * self.num_freqs)\n        cheb_points = np.cos(np.pi * np.flip(uni_points))\n        return freq_avg + freq_diff * cheb_points\n\n\n\"\"\" Source current profiles determined by user-supplied data on a plane.\"\"\"\n\n\nclass CustomFieldSource(FieldSource, PlanarSource):\n    \"\"\"Implements a source corresponding to an input dataset containing ``E`` and ``H`` fields,\n    using the equivalence principle to define the actual injected currents.\n\n     Notes\n     -----\n\n        For the injection to work as expected (i.e. to reproduce the required ``E`` and ``H`` fields),\n        the field data must decay by the edges of the source plane, or the source plane must span the entire\n        simulation domain and the fields must match the simulation boundary conditions.\n\n        The equivalent source currents are fully defined by the field components tangential to the\n        source plane. For e.g. source normal along ``z``, the normal components (``Ez`` and ``Hz``)\n        can be provided but will have no effect on the results, and at least one of the tangential\n        components has to be in the dataset, i.e. at least one of ``Ex``, ``Ey``, ``Hx``, and ``Hy``.\n\n        .. TODO add image here\n\n        ..\n            TODO is this generic? Only the field components tangential to the custom source plane are needed and used\n            in the simulation. Due to the equivalence principle, these fully define the currents that need to be\n            injected. This is not to say that the normal components of the data (:math:`E_x`, :math:`H_x` in our example)\n            is lost or not injected. It is merely not needed as it can be uniquely obtained using the tangential components.\n\n        ..\n            TODO add example for this standalone\n            Source data can be imported from file just as shown here, after the data is imported as a numpy array using\n            standard numpy functions like loadtxt.\n\n        If the data is not coming from a ``tidy3d`` simulation, the normalization is likely going to be arbitrary and\n        the directionality of the source will likely not be perfect, even if both the ``E`` and ``H`` fields are\n        provided. This can be\n        computed in our eigenmode solver :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver` and implement the mode simulation in\n        FDTD.\n\n        Mode sources are normalized to inject exactly 1W of power at the central frequency.\n\n        The modal source allows you to do directional excitation. Illustrated\n        by the image below, the field is perfectly launched to the right of the source and there's zero field to the\n        left of the source. Now you can contrast the behavior of the modal source with that of a dipole source. If\n        you just put a dipole into the waveguide, well, you see quite a bit different in the field distribution.\n        First of all, the dipole source is not directional launching. It launches waves in both directions. The\n        second is that the polarization of the dipole is set to selectively excite a TE mode. But it takes some\n        propagation distance before the mode settles into a perfect TE mode profile. During this process,\n        there is radiation into the substrate.\n\n        .. image:: /_static/img/mode_vs_dipole_source.png\n\n        **Practical Advice**\n\n        Place mode sources in waveguide sections with a uniform cross-section. The mode profile is\n        computed assuming translational invariance (or constant bend radius) along the injection axis.\n        For bent waveguides, set ``bend_radius`` and ``bend_axis`` accordingly.
